newsitem.title: NORWAY: New Norwegian premier is Labour Party product.
newsitem.headline: New Norwegian premier is Labour Party product.

text.p: Thorbjoern Jagland, named on Wednesday as successor to Norwegian prime minister Gro Harlem Brundtland, is a pure-bred product of the Labour Party, the country's most powerful political group.

Jagland, 46, groomed as Brundtland's heir-apparent, has spent his career moving through the ranks of the party, a centre-left movement that combines a passionate concern with social welfare and a strong interest in the personal wealth of Norwegians.

Recent opinion polls have shown that voters would turn their backs on the Labour Party with Jagland at the helm. But such surveys say more about Brundtland's standing with the Norwegian public than about distrust of Jagland.

"It is not easy to succeed a prime minister who has become the country's property. It may take time before Norway becomes on first-name terms with Thorbjoern as it has become with Gro," the national news agency NTB said.
Brundtland, 57, has dominated politics for 15 years.
Financial markets are wary of Jagland, who takes over from her on Friday.
His support for continued state ownership of industry and banks has won him few friends in the markets, which reacted nervously on Wednesday to the news of his appointment.
Jagland was born in Drammen, just west of the Norwegian capital Oslo, on November 5, 1950.
His first senior position came in 1977 as leader of the AUF, Labour's youth organisation.
In 1981, the year Brundtland first became prime minister, Jagland was busy building himself a powerbase in the party.
In 1992, he was voted in as leader of the party following Brundtland's resignation from the post after her son committed suicide.
The following year Jagland took over as parliamentary representative for the county of Buskerud.
While Brundtland worked extensively behind the scenes to carve out her policies, Jagland is seen as consulting widely on most issues.

Jagland is married with two sons, Anders and Henrik, and his family clearly comes first. Jagland turned down a golden chance to work in Brundtland's office in 1986 as a junior minister, saying he needed time with his children.
